newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: INTERVIEW-Asia faces new competitive era-Peregrine.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Asia faces new competitive era-Peregrine.

text.p: Asian economies undergoing a period of structural adjustments must cope with the trauma of a strong U.S. dollar but can look forward to some capital outflow from Japan, a top emerging markets specialist said on Wednesday.
Christopher Wood, a director of Hong Kong-based Peregrine Securities, told Reuters in an interview Asia should brace for a dollar/yen rate of around 110-120 in the medium-term.
Local currency strengths, if supported by dollar/yen, should also be welcome as they provide the incentive for economies to move their export industries up the value-added ladder, he said.
"The strong dollar trend is a deflationary influence for the Asia ex-Japan region," Wood said.
He said the pursuit of export-led growth on a weak dollar, as during the period prior to 1995, was over.

"Asian economies boomed on the back of the weak dollar as most of these countries, formally or informally, tended to peg their exchange rates against the U.S. denominated exchange rate basket," he said. This led to a great export-led boom based primarily on the U.S. consumer, he added.
The rising dollar since 1995, lifting Asian currencies with it, has resulted in less competitive exports.
Wood said the yen was likely to weaken to the 150 level against the dollar over the next 18 months.
"Japanese capital outflows out of Japan will be running at a greater level than the trade flow from the Japanese trade surplus," Wood said, noting this trend was already underway.
Liberalisation of foreign exchange laws in Japan from April 1 next year, and the current problems in its financial and insurance sectors, will trigger the capital flight.
"The Japanese can make higher returns overseas than they can at home because interest rates are very low and their dividend yields and stock market are very low," he said.
Asia could capture a new phase of portfolio capital, although this would not be huge direct investment of the kind that dominated the 1980s when Japanese companies built factories all over Asia.
Wood said Japanese investors had been mostly net sellers of Asian equities in the last two years, but pension money was clearly filtering into Asia now.
"Some money will be coming back to Asia, but we are not at the end of Asia's structural adjustment," Wood said, noting the economies here were sustaining "growing pains".
Excess production capacity, overheated property markets and indiscriminate lending by banks have plagued some economies.
"In the short-term you can get even more money in emerging market funds in Latin America than in Asia," Woods said.
The Asian region excluding Japan had been losing funds to hotter emerging areas, such as eastern Europe and Latin America, to the extent that asset allocation here has fallen, Wood said.
This, however, was part of a cyclical move and Asia would eventually return to favour, he said.
Meanwhile, in this difficult environment, Wood said he would bet on Hong Kong, China, Taiwan and emerging Asian countries such as India, Indonesia and the Philippines.

He said Hong Kong was not an expensive market and was fuelled by the red chip phenomenon -- Hongkong incorporated companies with Chinese financial backing -- while China was experiencing low inflation that could spur liquidity for the stock market.
